summary: Describes how DNS SRV records, DNS TXT records, and well-known URIs can be used, together or separately, to locate CalDAV calendar and CardDAV contact services. This lets clients find servers from just a domain name or address. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: If you want to find a school's calendar, you should not have to guess its address. This memo explains the clues to look up so your app finds it on its own.

questions: what is the caldav well-known uri
what is the txt path key for caldav
subtitle: How a calendar or contacts app can find a CalDAV or CardDAV server from just an address and password.

tldr.problem: CalDAV and CardDAV clients need to find servers without users knowing the server's fully qualified domain name, port or the path where the service lives.
tldr.mechanism: DNS SRV records give the host and port, an optional DNS TXT record gives the path, and the well-known URIs /.well-known/caldav and /.well-known/carddav redirect to the real path. A step-by-step client bootstrapping procedure ties them together.
tldr.outcome: A client can configure itself from a calendar user address or email address and a password. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 4791 and RFC 6352.

today: RFC 6764 is a Proposed Standard from February 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 4791 (CalDAV) and RFC 6352 (CardDAV).

sections.title: The Discovery Problem
sections.content:
RFC 4791 defines CalDAV, a calendar access protocol based on HTTP, and RFC 6352 defines CardDAV for contacts. Clients need to find suitable servers on their local network and at other domains, so that users do not have to know details such as the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) and port number.

RFC 2782 defines DNS SRV records for locating services, and RFC 6763 adds service metadata in TXT records. This RFC defines the new SRV service types for CalDAV; the CardDAV ones were already defined in RFC 6352.

SRV records only give an FQDN and port, not a path. A service may live below a context path such as /caldav/ rather than at the root of the server, so clients also need a way to learn that path. This RFC uses the well-known URI feature of RFC 5785 for that.
sections.eli5: Knowing which building a library is in is not enough. You also need to know which room. This memo gives your app clues for both.

sections.title: SRV Labels and the TXT Path Key
sections.content:
Two SRV service labels are added for CalDAV: _caldav for HTTP without TLS and _caldavs for HTTP with TLS. Clients MUST honor the Priority and Weight values in SRV records. Examples from the RFC are _caldav._tcp SRV 0 1 80 calendar.example.com. and _caldavs._tcp SRV 0 1 443 calendar.example.com..

A site may also publish a TXT record next to the SRV record. It follows the syntax of RFC 6763 and defines a path key whose value MUST be the actual context path, as in _caldavs._tcp TXT path=/caldav. When present, clients MUST use that value as the context path. When it is absent, clients use the well-known URI approach.
sections.eli5: The first clue says which computer to call and which door to knock on. A second optional clue says which room inside to walk to.

sections.title: The Well-Known URIs
sections.content:
The RFC registers two well-known URIs, caldav and carddav. They point to a resource a client can use as its initial context path. The server MUST redirect HTTP requests for it to the real context path, for example with a 301, 303 or 307 response, and clients MUST handle such redirects. Servers MUST NOT place the real service endpoint at the well-known URI itself.

Servers SHOULD set a suitable Cache-Control header on the redirect. For instance, if the redirect target may change over time, a no-cache value fits. To allow per-user paths, a server MAY require authentication on the well-known URI, answering 401 first and sending the redirect only after the client authenticates.

In the RFC's example the context path is /servlet/caldav. The client requests /.well-known/caldav, receives a redirect whose Location is /servlet/caldav, follows it and carries on.
sections.eli5: It is like a sign at a fixed spot that always says "the calendar desk has moved, go there". The sign never changes, even if the desk does.

sections.title: Client Bootstrapping Procedure
sections.content:
Clients SHOULD follow a procedure whose goal is an http: or https: URI for the user's principal-URL. It starts from minimal input. For CalDAV that is a calendar user address (a URI, such as a mailto: address) and a password; for CardDAV it is an email address and a password. The user identifier and domain are extracted from it.

  1. Find host and port. Look up _caldavs._tcp (or _carddavs._tcp) for the domain. If nothing is found, the client can try the non-TLS label, provided non-TLS connections are appropriate. Multiple records are ordered by Priority and Weight. With no SRV record, the client can ask the user or use the domain as the FQDN with default ports, and MUST first attempt a TLS connection.
  2. Find the context path. After a valid SRV result the client MUST also query the TXT record and use its path value if present. Otherwise the path is /.well-known/caldav or /.well-known/carddav. If a TXT-derived path gives HTTP errors, the client SHOULD retry with the well-known URI.
  3. Find the user identifier. For a mailto: address the client MUST first use the mailbox portion, and if authentication fails SHOULD fall back to the local part. For http: or https: addresses the userinfo is used.
  4. Connect. With the TLS labels, negotiation happens immediately and the client MUST verify the certificate per RFC 6125. The client sends a PROPFIND (RFC 4918) to the context path, asking for DAV:current-user-principal, and MUST handle redirects. On a 404 it MAY try the root URI / or ask the user. If the property comes back, a further PROPFIND on the principal-URL reveals calendar or address book home collections; if not, the user must supply the principal-URL path.

After success, clients SHOULD cache the service details. If connection or authentication later fails persistently, they SHOULD repeat the SRV lookup and account discovery to refresh the cache.
sections.eli5: Your app reads your email address, looks up where its server lives, asks the server to point to your own calendar, and then remembers the way for next time.

sections.title: Guidance for Service Providers
sections.content:
Providers who want clients to auto-configure need to follow several rules. Servers SHOULD accept authentication with calendar user addresses (or email addresses for CardDAV) or with identifiers extracted from them. Addresses MUST NOT conflict with other permitted login names, and extracted identifiers must be unique across the server and MUST NOT conflict with any login name.

Servers MUST force authentication for PROPFIND requests that retrieve DAV:current-user-principal, so that the returned value is the principal-URL of the requesting user. If TLS is used, a certificate that clients can verify as described in RFC 6125 MUST be installed, and it SHOULD include SRV-ID and DNS-ID identifiers as appropriate. Providers should install the right SRV records and may add TXT records.
sections.eli5: If you run the calendar service, make sure each person can log in with their email, that the server only shows people their own stuff, and that the lock on the door is the right one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clients that support TLS SHOULD try _caldavs or _carddavs before the non-TLS labels. If a user explicitly asked for TLS, the client MUST NOT use service information from _caldav or _carddav. Clients MUST follow the certificate verification process of RFC 6125.

An attacker who controls DNS data, or who gets spoofed answers cached in a recursive resolver, could steer clients to any server. Without a secure DNS option, clients SHOULD check that the SRV target FQDN lies in the domain they queried, and otherwise SHOULD confirm with the user before connecting. With TLS, clients MUST check the SRV-ID in the server certificate when the target differs from the queried domain; when it matches, they check SRV-ID identifiers, or DNS-ID identifiers if no SRV-ID is present. Clients and servers MUST NOT request, offer or use SSL 2.0.
sections.eli5: A trickster could swap the signpost to send you to the wrong place. So your app checks the new place looks like it belongs to the right owner, and asks you if it does not.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers the well-known URI suffixes caldav and carddav, with the IETF as change controller. It also registers four service names for TCP: caldav (non-TLS) and caldavs (over TLS), defined here, and carddav and carddavs, defined in RFC 6352. The non-TLS names are extensions of the http service and the TLS names of the https service, and all four list the TXT key path=<context path>.
sections.eli5: The official list of service names now has entries for the calendar and contacts services, with and without the lock.
